description_full: Pentair plc provides various water solutions in the United States, Western Europe, China, Latin America, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Australia, and Canada. It operates through three segments: Flow, Water Solutions, and Pool. The Flow segment designs, manufactures, and sells fluid treatment and pump products and systems, including pressure vessels, gas recovery solutions, membrane bioreactors, wastewater reuse systems and advanced membrane filtration, separation systems, specialty insertion valves, water disposal pumps, water supply pumps, fluid transfer pumps, turbine pumps, solid handling pumps, and agricultural spray nozzles. This segment provides products under Pentair Flow, Aurora, Berkeley, Codeline, Fairbanks-Nijhuis, Haffmans, Hydromatic, Hypro, Jung Pumpen, Myers, Sta-Rite, Shurflo, Südmo, and X-Flow brand names. The Water Solutions segment offers commercial and residential water treatment products and systems, such as pressure tanks, control valves, activated carbon products, commercial ice machines, conventional filtration products, and point-of-entry and point-of-use water treatment systems for use in water filtration and water softening solutions, as well as commercial water management and filtration solutions in foodservice operations; and installation and preventative services for water management solutions for commercial operators under the Pentair Water Solutions, Everpure, Fleck, Manitowoc Ice, Pentek, and RainSoft brands. The Pool segment provides residential and commercial pool equipment and accessories, including pumps, filters, heaters, lights, automatic controls and cleaners, chlorinators, maintenance equipment, and pool accessories for residential and commercial pool maintenance, pool repair, renovation, service, construction, and aquaculture solutions. This segment offers products under the Pentair Pool, Kreepy Krauly, Pleatco, and Sta-Rite brands. Pentair plc was founded in 1966 and is headquartered in London, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: Pentair plc. is a large-cap industrials business with a $10.9B market cap on $4.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +0% over the past three years and -4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 14% against a 9% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 35%.

The business throws off $746M in free cash flow — roughly 18 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.25× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.8× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.7×.

Shareholder yield of 3.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Goodwill represents 52% of total assets — a large impairment risk hanging over book value
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Price sits 21% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Above-average short interest at 5.5% of float
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 12% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
35 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 21% operating margin runs 12pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.84x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 50% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 37% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 37% and a beta of 1.08, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.29 vs 5y 1.09), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $152.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 45% in the 2022 bear market and 55% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $56.42 (margin of safety -21%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 16%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $44.35 to $71.50 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 18.6 vs 24.1 and P/FCF 14.6 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 16% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $73.73 on average, 8% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 9.3%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.55).
It runs a 35% gross margin and converts 18% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.25x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.3% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA ($74.0M of cash against $1.6B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 10.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.9, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 52% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 0.4% over 3 years, 6.7% over 5 years and -4.3% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 24%).
At current returns, reinvesting 7% of profits supports about 0.9% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 7.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a backlog worth 2% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 11%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 1.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 24, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (1.0%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 3.6% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks and 1.6% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 35 consecutive years, raising it 5.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 9,000 employees, each generates about $464K of revenue, 1.3x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 2.2% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $83K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.0M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
